name: Amira Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the disability support team at the Riverside benefits centre. Most of my day is reading medical evidence, so doctors' letters, care plans, sometimes forty pages for one person, and working out which bits match the rules for daily living support. Graham, my team leader, signs off anything complicated, which with me is still most things. I live on my own in a studio above a laundrette, so my flat always smells of fabric softener, which I've decided is a perk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a case clicks, when you find the line in a consultant's letter that proves someone can't cook a meal safely. What wears me out is the reconsiderations, when people ask us to look again and I can hear in their voice they've been crying. Some weeks I take that home with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right for us, to be fair. We got a summary tool last spring and it's handy, but it still misses things a nurse would spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about proper staffing and proper training. I'd probably post something like AI was never going to fix a system that was underfunded. My friends would roll their eyes because I say that about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd be glad. I'm not good enough at this job yet to want the ground moving under me. The summary tool takes maybe twenty minutes off a long case, and that's all I want from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the summary tool for long files, but always read the doctor's letters myself. I'd ask Graham to put me on the training for complex cases this spring. And I'd keep my savings where they are, about four months, because my landlord's already hinted the rent's going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with the rent nagging at me. The job feels safe enough. It's the cost of living above a laundrette in a city that keeps getting pricier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the summary tool misses things. What sort of things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It skips the small lines that matter. The summary tool will tell you someone has arthritis, but it won't notice the doctor wrote that she can't open a jar. That's the line that wins the case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the rent going up mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably fifty a month more, and I'd absorb it. I'd stop the gym and do the free run on Saturdays instead. It's annoying, not scary.

say: I'd say the real fix is **staffing and training**, not more software.
I'd post that AI could never fix an **underfunded system** on its own.
think: I'm glad, because I'm **not skilled enough** yet to want big change.
The **summary tool** saves twenty minutes on long cases, which is enough.
do: Keep using the summary tool but **read every doctor's letter** myself.
Ask my team leader for **complex-case training** this spring.
Hold savings at about **four months** ahead of a rent rise.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with the **rising rent** nagging at her.
S0.quote: The summary tool will tell you someone has arthritis, but it won't notice the doctor wrote that she can't open a jar.
fieldNote: She already uses AI a little and is **comfortable** with it as a helper.
Her main pressure is **housing costs**, not her job, in this picture.
She values **small details** in medical evidence that she thinks machines miss.

steps.text: Keep using the summary tool on long files, checking every letter
Ask Graham for a place on the complex-case training
Swap the gym for the free Saturday run to cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's closer to what I'm scared of. Checking and writing is basically the whole disability team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the union earns its money. We need agreements on how many staff a tool replaces and what happens to them. I'd say it at team meetings, politely, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they'd move us from deciding to reviewing what the tool decides. That sounds fine until there are half as many of us. And the people reviewing would be the experienced ones, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person on my team who's good at the new tools, because that's a reason to keep me. I'd go to the union's sessions on new technology agreements. And I'd move from saving fifty a month to a hundred and fifty, and get to six months before anything happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do with my hands, so to speak. I do better when I've got a plan. It's the waiting that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean towards public support and unions. Do you see any good in this for claimants?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tools cut the backlog, yes. People wait eleven weeks for a decision right now. If an AI tool gets a disabled man his money in two weeks instead of eleven, I can't honestly be against it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Leila, she's a nurse, she's watched the same thing happen with their records system. She'd tell me to stop catastrophising and make a list. Then Josie at work, who'd want to go to the pub and complain first.

say: I'd say the union must agree **how many staff** a tool replaces.
I'd raise it **politely but firmly** at team meetings.
think: Caseworkers would shift from deciding to **reviewing the tool**, with fewer of us.
The **experienced staff** would do the reviewing, not juniors like me.
do: Become my team's **go-to person** for the new AI tools.
Attend the union's sessions on **technology agreements**.
Save **a hundred and fifty** a month to reach six months.
feel: **Anxious**, but calmer once she has a **plan** to follow.
S1.quote: If an AI tool gets a disabled man his money in two weeks instead of eleven, I can't honestly be against it.
fieldNote: She holds two views: AI could **help claimants** and threaten her post.
Her strategy is to be **useful with the tools**, not to resist them.
Her sister Leila acts as her **practical anchor** when she spirals.

steps.text: Volunteer to test the new decision tool and train teammates
Join the union's sessions on technology agreements
Raise savings to a hundred and fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. I'd still be on the junior grade in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a guarantee that nobody loses their income overnight, something like a basic income or full pay while you retrain. I'd say it everywhere, and I'd mean it. This is exactly what government is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone. Reading medical evidence and matching it to rules is exactly what this AI would do better than me. Maybe a few people stay on to talk to claimants, but they'd be the senior ones. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me, because I don't do anything with my hands at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Leila about moving into her spare room so I could stop paying rent and stretch my savings. I'd apply for a nursing assistant course, because care work is hands-on and that buys me about three years. And I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for income protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. I'm twenty-seven, I only just got a real job, and it would feel like losing it before I'd even learned it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nursing, when you've said care work only buys you three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because three years is three years, and Leila says there's always a shortage. And honestly, I'm not sure people want a robot washing their mum. I'd rather bet on people wanting a human hand than bet on a desk job that's already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio. Losing the laundrette smell would be the saddest bit, I know that's silly. After that, the trips home to see my parents, because the train's expensive.

say: I'd demand that **nobody loses income** overnight, through basic income or paid retraining.
I'd say income protection is **exactly what government** is for.
think: My job **reading medical evidence** is precisely what this AI would do better.
The **robot delay** doesn't help me, because none of my work is hands-on.
do: Move into my **sister's spare room** to stretch my savings.
Apply for a **nursing assistant** course to buy about three years.
feel: **Alarmed** and lying awake about losing a job she has barely learned.
S2.quote: I'd rather bet on people wanting a human hand than bet on a desk job that's already gone.
fieldNote: She sees **no hands-on buffer** in her own job, so the date hits her directly.
Care work appeals as a **human-touch** job robots may not be welcome in.
Her **sister's support** is her main safety net beyond savings.

steps.text: Move into Leila's spare room and give up the studio
Apply for a nursing assistant course at the city college
Join a campaign pushing for income protection

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels like something I could actually use. Not easy, but usable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say use the five years well: train public staff now, not when the letters come. I'd write to my local representative about it, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time to get one qualification before it hits. Not a long one. I'd want to land in work where the person matters more than the paperwork, and the robot part comes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time social work degree next autumn, evenings and weekends, while keeping the caseworker job. I'd use the AI tools at work as much as they'd let me, so I'm not useless if I stay. And I'd keep saving the hundred and fifty a month, because the degree costs money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but determined. It's a lot of evenings. But I'd feel like I'm doing something rather than watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Social work is still a lot of thinking work. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. But it's sitting in kitchens and noticing things, and deciding with a family, not just for them. A social worker in someone's kitchen notices the empty fridge, and no report the AI writes will ever smell like that kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a part-time loan, and the department sometimes funds staff on related courses. I'd ask Graham straight away. If they say no, I'd still do it and eat a lot of lentils.

say: I'd say **train public staff** now, not when redundancy letters arrive.
I'd write to my **local representative** for the first time in my life.
think: I'd have time for **one qualification** before AGI arrives.
I want work where **the person matters** more than the paperwork.
do: Start a **part-time social work degree** next autumn while keeping my job.
Use the **AI tools** at work as much as allowed.
Keep saving **a hundred and fifty** a month for course costs.
feel: **Anxious but determined**, glad to be acting instead of watching.
S3.quote: A social worker in someone's kitchen notices the empty fridge, and no report the AI writes will ever smell like that kitchen.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **concrete plan** with one qualification.
She knows social work is **still thinking work** but values its human presence.
She is **willing to self-fund** even if the department says no.

steps.text: Start a part-time social work degree next autumn
Use the AI tools at work as much as Graham allows
Write to her local representative about staff retraining
Keep saving a hundred and fifty a month for fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd probably be in a different job anyway. People move around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade, so there's no excuse for chaos. Plan the transition, protect the claimants, and look after the staff. I'd say it in a slightly smug voice because I'd finally have time to be organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd probably be all right if I actually did the work. But AGI is still AGI. Even social work would change by the end, so I'd be planning for a moving target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the complex-case training, then do the social work degree over four years at a gentle pace. I'd keep my savings growing slowly and maybe get a flatmate. And I'd learn the AI tools properly, because in ten years everyone will use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still a bit anxious, but in the background. More like a deadline than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could tell your thirty-seven-year-old self one thing, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't wait for permission. Ten years of warning is only useful if I start in the first year, not the ninth. I know what I'm like with deadlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the longer time change anything outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd stop renting alone and buy somewhere small with a partner, if there's a partner by then. With two years I wouldn't touch a mortgage. With ten, I might take the risk.

say: I'd say a decade means **no excuse for chaos** in the transition.
I'd call for plans that **protect claimants** and look after staff.
think: I'd probably be **all right** if I actually did the work.
Even **social work** would change by the end, so it's a moving target.
do: Finish complex-case training, then a four-year **social work degree**.
Learn the **AI tools** properly and grow savings slowly with a flatmate.
feel: **Background anxiety**, more like a **deadline** than a cliff.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is only useful if I start in the first year, not the ninth.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **pace** retraining, but she still expects her job to change.
She knows she **procrastinates** and wants to start in year one.
Buying a home only feels possible with **long warning**.

steps.text: Finish complex-case training, then start the social work degree
Take the department's full AI tools course
Find a flatmate to keep savings growing slowly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because it's the ending I fear most, but because I'd be caught halfway through learning a job that's disappearing. What would help is paid retraining, real money while you study, so I'm not choosing between rent and a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether anyone asks claimants. Everyone talks about staff, which is me, fine. The people I'm most worried about are the ones on my caseload, who can't argue with a computer that says no.

headlineQuote: The people I'm most worried about are the ones on my caseload, who can't argue with a computer that says no.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** junior disability support caseworker who lives alone above a laundrette.
She uses AI tools **now and then** and believes in unions and public support.
She goes from **uneasy** about rent in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028.
Her plan is **retraining** into social work or care, leaning on her nurse sister Leila.
She worries about **claimants** facing automated decisions as much as about her own job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, catching her halfway through learning a job that is disappearing.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with real income during study, so rent and courses don't compete.
